title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 111
paragraphs: Now Artybius was riding a horse that had been trained to rear up against a hoplite. Onesilus, on being informed of this, and having a shield-bearer by race a Carian who was of very good repute as a soldier and full of courage besides, said to this man: “I am informed that the horse of Artybius rears upright and works both with his hooves and his mouth against anyone he is brought to attack. Consider the matter, then, and tell me at once which of the two you would rather watch for and strike, the horse or Artybius himself.” His attendant replied: “O king, I am ready to do both or either of these, and in every case to do what you appoint for me; but I will tell you the way I think most suitable for your condition. I say it is right that one who is a king and commander should fight with a king and commander; for if you kill the enemy's commander, it turns to great glory for you; and again, if he kills you—which heaven forbid—even death, when it is at the hands of a worthy foe, is only half to be lamented. As for us who are under your command, it is fitting that we fight with the others under his command and with his horse. And of the horse's tricks have no fear at all, for I promise you that after this at least he shall never stand against any man again.” So he spoke; and shortly afterwards the opposing forces joined battle both on land and with their ships.
